messages.subject: openCR survival interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Happy New Year!

I am Hongli Yu. I am currently modelling the survival of hedgehogs with an 11-year SCR dataset using openCR 2.2.5, CJS. I am not quite sure how to interpret the results (shown below), and could anyone help with this please? Thank you in advance!

Basic information: hedgehogs were classed as juveniles (year of born) and adults (survived for at least one winter; the majority were classified as adults when they were first caught). Our search area was about 10 times male adult’s normal home range(~20ha), but most captures were from the central area, and only a small number were from areas close to the edge (despite the comparable search effort). I fitted models for female adults, male adults, female adults and juveniles combined, and male adults and juveniles combined separately. When adults and juveniles combined, they shared all the parameters (as the detection p~age did not work well). Then based on the AIC, across these groups the constant survival models (phi~1) were more supported than year/session-specific (phi ~t), and the Spatial normal movement models were more supported than the Spatial static.

My questions are: can I understand that the Movement kernel scale α is the estimated average distance of activity centers across individuals between years? The α was almost identical for adult males and adult females; but when juveniles were further added, it became higher in males (adult juvenile combined, 354 m, 95% CI 193 - 648) than that in females (adult juvenile combined, 180m, 95% CI 1 - 326), likely indicating the possible natal dispersal in related to males from their born year to their second year? Indeed, all juvenile males were not recaptured after July of their second year, compared to 76% of juvenile females). Further, is the survival from spatial normal (e.g., 0.447 for male adult juvenile combined) minus that from spatial static (0.442) relevant to the migration rate? If so, then this seems to be very low?

Thank you very much! Any help would be very appreciated!

Kind regards,

Hongli Yu, PhD student

Nottingham Trent University, UK

hongli...@my.ntu.ac.uk

hongli...@gmail.com

messages.subject: Re: openCR survival interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Hello Hongli Yu
Open-population SECR is a bit of a minefield as you've found: results from real-world (modest-sized) datasets don't always 'make sense'.

You mention CJS, but there is no direct spatial analogue of CJS. Type CJSsecr produces nonsense unless you set CJSp1 to TRUE to model first captures, and then you may as well fit one of the models with recruitment.

We can be almost certain that a bivariate normal movement model is inferior to one with longer tails e.g. BVE or RDE (see MEE review 2022).

The parameter 'a' of the movement model does not equate with average distance moved - you need to get this later see e.g. ?summary.kernel

The pattern of sex-biased natal dispersal in your hedgehogs seems very plausible. As I interpret it, all locally born males had disappeared by the second year? Modelling long-distance emigration is going to be hard (impossible with this scale of sampling?), and a BVN model doesn't help. I wouldn't make anything of the difference in survival rates between static and bivariate normal models.

Hope this helps despite being a bit gloomy!
Murray

messages.subject: Discretized model instead of area search model?
messages.subject_clean: Discretized model instead of area search model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am Marina Ramon. I am trying to estimate chimpanzee density using genetic data from faecal samples. I am using CL models for area searches. The area searched has a complex shape (i.e. ~ 50 polygons grouping searched cells) and this makes the model fitting very slow.

As an alternative, I tried a CL model for count detectors after discretization, which allowed me to fit the model much more quickly. The complex shape of the area searched already required me to define the search area as a subset of cells within a regular grid, so it was straightforward to treat the centroid of each searched cell as a detector. Estimates from one successfully-fitted area search model matched those from the discretized model (the density estimates were practically identical).

So far, I’ve tried with null models, but now I would like to incorporate covariates and also try to fit an h2 model. I was thinking of using a CL model for count detectors instead of a CL model for area searches to make sure I can fit the models. How appropriate would be to treat data from area searches as if they arose from an array of detectors?

Thank you very much in advance.

Marina

messages.subject: Problem with my N-Mixture model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am stuckwith my n-mixture model for wolved from cameratrap data.

Of course it is a elusive species so, I get NAs in some of the sampling stations.

I am not getting succesful goodness of fit. I get some very weird outliers. As the one showed down here. I also get very high c-hat values, indicating data Overdispersion in P, NB but not in ZIP.

Also attached my “counts” data structure as an indicator of how much NAs are present.

I have tried with raw environmental data and with standardized environmental data, with similar results.

Can anyone tell what I could be doing wrong? Is there any particular treatment I should apply to NAs or stations with all zeros.

Thank you in advance.

```
WolfCounts <- list(sites = sites,dates = dates,dur = dur,counts = counts)
y0 <- as.matrix(WolfCounts$counts[,-1])
dimnames(y0) <- list(sites = sites$Site, rep = colnames(WolfCounts$counts)[2:ncol(WolfCounts$counts)])

y <- y0

time <- matrix(rep(as.character(1:9), nrow(y)), ncol = 9, byrow = TRUE)
umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y = y,
                           siteCovs=data.frame(elev=scale(sites[,"elevation"]), dist.wat=scale(sites[,"wat.dist"]),
                                              dist.pop=scale(sites[,"pop.dist"]), days= 1/(sites[,"days"])),
                           obsCovs=list(time = time, date = scale(date), dur = scale(dur)))

fm2 <- pcount(~ (elev + I(elev^2)) * (dist.pop + I(dist.pop^2)) + time-1
              - I(dist.pop^2)
              ~ (elev + I(elev^2)) * (dist.wat + I(dist.wat^2)) + days
              - I(elev^2):dist.wat,
              umf, control=list(trace=TRUE, REPORT=5, maxit = 300), K=800)

fm2NB <- pcount(fm2@formula,
                umf, control=list(trace=TRUE, REPORT=5), K=1000, mixture = "NB”)

fm2ZIP <- pcount(fm2@formula,
                 umf, control=list(trace=TRUE, REPORT=5), K=800, mixture = "ZIP")

```

Antonio Sampedro Garrido
Biologist and Tibetan Language Translator

messages.subject_clean: Problem with Telemetry and Impervious Surface Covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am in the last little bit of my project here and have been cruising but I hit a snag with using impervious raster as a covariate on D while incorporating telemetry.

I successfully used D~ impervious surface on fDNA models only but once I added in my telemetry data to the ms.capthist, I am getting high densities, NAs on SE and CIs, and small sigma. It also outputs a ton of warnings.

I'm not sure what is happening here. Maybe the covariate is not using telemetry to supplement sigma only. or the addCovariate could be reading in wrong even though it plots correctly.

The end goal here is to use predictDsurface on the model output. Does anyone have experience using all these things together?

I am happy to provide code and files offline.

Thanks, Ashley

messages.subject_clean: Discretized model instead of area search model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi
As you reported, the two approaches (polygon search, polygon discretized as point many detectors) can give very similar estimates. I would expect this to hold even for covariate models. There will be some differences in the covariate effects themselves if you are talking about detector-level covariates, but that seems unlikely. Occasion and individual covariates of detection parameters should be fine. Also spatial covariates of density if you leave CL behind.
Murray

> Hi
> As you reported, the two approaches (polygon search, polygon discretized as point many detectors) can give very similar estimates. I would expect this to hold even for covariate models. There will be some differences in the covariate effects themselves if you are talking about detector-level covariates, but that seems unlikely. Occasion and individual covariates of detection parameters should be fine. Also spatial covariates of density if you leave CL behind.
> Murray

> > I am Marina Ramon. I am trying to estimate chimpanzee density using genetic data from faecal samples. I am using CL models for area searches. The area searched has a complex shape (i.e. ~ 50 polygons grouping searched cells) and this makes the model fitting very slow.
> >
> >
> >
> > As an alternative, I tried a CL model for count detectors after discretization, which allowed me to fit the model much more quickly. The complex shape of the area searched already required me to define the search area as a subset of cells within a regular grid, so it was straightforward to treat the centroid of each searched cell as a detector. Estimates from one successfully-fitted area search model matched those from the discretized model (the density estimates were practically identical).
> >
> >
> >
> > So far, I’ve tried with null models, but now I would like to incorporate covariates and also try to fit an h2 model. I was thinking of using a CL model for count detectors instead of a CL model for area searches to make sure I can fit the models. How appropriate would be to treat data from area searches as if they arose from an array of detectors?
> >

> >
> >
> > Marina
